R2-01.why: A human Parent hunting human kids makes each round play out differently, as Granny and Flee the Facility show, and three phases plus snitching give each session variety. But a fixed set of 60 hotspots per house, plus a Collection Log that rewards finding them all, turns the Parent's job into a memorised sweep within about 10 rounds.
R2-01.fix: Let only a random 30-40% of hotspots exist each round and let kids create temporary decoy hotspots, so the Parent reads players instead of checking a list; drop the 'find all 60' log for a log of moments/feats.

R2-02.why: The fun of co-ordinating paddles comes early: once a crew syncs up, there is little left to master, and bots in seats remove the chaos the game depends on. Daily seeds and new vehicles every two weeks add novelty rather than depth, and the vehicle schedule costs a small team a lot.
R2-02.fix: Add a skill ceiling: per-segment line choices, shortcut branches that need precise co-ordination, and a vs mode where rafts sabotage each other mid-river, so a good crew keeps finding faster lines.

R2-03.why: Bluffing as a statue among about 30 NPCs whose poses shift gives real human-reading depth, and the flashlight battery creates guard decisions. But glowing prank targets on known museum wings become a fixed route, and one 4-minute rule set gets repetitive, a known weakness of Be-NPC-or-Die games.
R2-03.fix: Randomise which pranks are live and hide some (find-them-first), add statue abilities that create real misdirection, and give the Guard a ranked ladder with per-match stat cards so the guard role grows in skill.

R2-04.why: A roguelite with relic drafts, weekly mutators and ranked seeds is a strong replay engine, and timing fusions with friends adds co-op skill. Limits: only six runes, a fusion book that empties once it's discovered, the gesture novelty wearing off, and no movement keeping tactical depth shallow.
R2-04.fix: Make relics change how fusions behave (build-defining synergies), add enemy types that demand specific fusions, and grow the rune set each season so the draft space keeps growing after the Rune Book is done.

R2-05.why: Social deduction has proven replay because other players change every game (Among Us, MM2). But inspection tells that glow under the right tool become a checklist fast, and with chat gated for under-16s, a stamp-only Appraisal Meeting leaves the deduction layer thin.
R2-05.fix: Have forgers choose which tells to fake (a hidden budget) so inspection becomes a bluffing duel, and build richer non-chat evidence (timelines, alibi stamps, accuse/defend emotes).

R2-06.why: Anomaly games are the clearest case of 'memorised content becomes a checklist': once seen, an anomaly loses its scare, and procedural anomalies built from primitives (swap/tint/move) read as generic rather than surprising. The Watcher/Patroller split adds a few nights of novelty, and the lane is the most crowded.
R2-06.fix: Make the Watcher able to lie (an occasional possessed/traitor Watcher) or add escalating threat AI, so the replay comes from trust and pressure rather than spotting new anomalies.

R2-07.why: Content Warning-style replay depends on fresh shenanigans plus a reveal, which is very funny the first few times; Content Warning's own audience fell off steeply after launch. A small ghost catalogue and a recorded best-30-seconds become routine, and progression (subscribers, gear) is shallow.
R2-07.fix: Add ghost behaviours that combine into new situations, objective-driven contracts with a risk/reward choice (go deeper for bigger shots), and a weekly community 'best clip' ladder.

R2-08.why: Per-parcel handling rules and linked carries give some Overcooked-like co-op skill, and procedural neighbourhoods help, but once the rule set is learned the parcels are solved. Shifts of three deliveries lack the escalating chaos and star-chasing that keep Overcooked going.
R2-08.fix: Combine parcel rules with hazards (a cake plus a sprinkler plus stairs), add star tiers per neighbourhood seed, and add a combo/streak multiplier so expert crews chase routes.

R2-09.why: The strongest long-term engine here: breeding with inheritance gives effectively endless goals that are your own, a data-driven log of 150 mutations is cheap to extend, and auto-battler placement plus one timed tap per round give fresh match-to-match decisions with a ranked season. Risks are a shallow 3-critter, 3x3 board and the power bar making outcomes feel decided.
R2-09.fix: Normalise power in ranked (trait synergies over raw stats) so breeding gives options rather than strength, and add between-round shop/positioning decisions so matches don't feel decided before they start.

R2-10.why: The Keep Talking structure is memorisation at its core: once a pair learns the pictographic manual, modules become a checklist, and a seasonal rulebook rotation is too slow to stop that. Depending on a 2-player group also limits how often it gets replayed.
R2-10.fix: Randomise the manual per device (symbol-to-action mapping shuffled every round) and scale difficulty with rule chaining and time pressure, so relaying stays a live skill rather than recall.

R2-11.why: Cascading Overcooked-style failures create emergent chaos, and rotating roles plus several vehicles add variety, but the routes are semi-scripted, the event set is finite, and the pitch has no stated star or score system or difficulty curve. Thinly specified compared with the others.
R2-11.fix: Generate emergencies from a director AI with escalating difficulty tiers, add per-route star scoring and daily seeds, and add role-specific skill (a pilot making route choices that set crew load).

R2-12.why: Fire spreading on a server grid through procedural buildings makes each run play out differently, alarm tiers 1-5 give skill progression, and a visitable sanctuary with 120 critters gives long-term goals plus a social space. Auto-aimed hoses keep the skill ceiling low, and critters that are fixed per building type become a checklist.
R2-12.fix: Add skill to firefighting (water/pressure management, ventilation, backdraft risk) and make rare critters appear under performance conditions (fast, no casualties at high alarm) rather than on fixed spawns.

overall_notes: Asked 'why play this 20 times?', the strongest answers come from long-term goals players set themselves combined with matches that vary (R2-09 breeding plus auto-battler), human opponents (R2-01, R2-05, R2-03) or roguelite/systemic variety (R2-04, R2-12). The weakest designs rely on content that gets memorised (anomalies, Keep Talking manuals, ghost catalogues) or on a novelty that wears off (synced paddling). Several concepts lean on collection logs that are themselves checklists; logs should reward feats rather than the exhaustive finding of fixed content. None reaches 9-10: none shows proven depth at the level of top-1% D7 retention, and the 8 for R2-09 depends on keeping breeding balanced so it isn't pay-to-win. Small-team scalability is best for data-driven content (mutations, relics, fire grid) and worst for hand-made vehicles/houses on a fixed schedule.
